payload.scope: A criterion of control and systems theory made so engineers can test whether a transfer function is positive-real, the passivity certificate that the KYP lemma and passivity-based feedback design consume.

definition.body: The positive-real property is the map systems theory draws over transfer functions: a proper transfer function G(s) is positive-real when Re G(jw) is nonnegative for every real frequency w at which G is defined, its imaginary-axis poles are simple, and their residues are positive; it is strictly positive-real when the real part is positive everywhere on the axis. The property is the category the discipline keeps, not the systems that satisfy it: the line is drawn by the frequency-domain inequality itself, against the neighbouring lines of positive-stability (all poles in the open left half-plane) and of positive-realness restricted to minimum-phase, and the category persists through systems theory texts that teach it as the passivity certificate, the KYP lemma that converts it to a linear matrix inequality in the state-space matrices, and the named check isposreal of the MATLAB System Identification Toolbox. e.g.: the isposreal check of a state-space model in the MATLAB System Identification Toolbox; the positive-realness condition in the KYP lemma of Zhou-Doyle-Glover (1996); the impedance of a lossless LC network, a positive-real function in the classical circuit texts | not: the positive-real lemma (the LMI equivalence that tests it); passivity (the energy-storage property it certifies); minimum-phase (no right-half-plane zeros, a different line) [formal: functio realis positiva | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

payload.name: griffin-lim-iteration
payload.scope: An iterative algorithm made to reconstruct a time-domain signal from magnitude spectrogram by alternately projecting onto time-domain consistency and magnitude constraints.

definition.body: Griffin-Lim iteration is an iterative phase-retrieval algorithm that reconstructs a time-domain signal from a magnitude spectrogram by alternately projecting onto the set of signals with the given magnitude spectrogram and the set of signals with consistent short-time Fourier transform properties. Each iteration computes the STFT of the current estimate, replaces the magnitude with the target magnitude, applies inverse STFT, and repeats. Parameters: (1) number of iterations; (2) STFT window length and hop size; (3) initialization method. It persists as a standard phase retrieval technique in audio synthesis, implemented in libraries such as librosa.griffinlim and scipy.signal. e.g.: librosa.griffinlim used to reconstruct audio from a magnitude spectrogram in music information retrieval demos; Griffin-Lim iteration in the MIRToolbox for spectrogram inversion; the Griffin-Lim algorithm in the phase retrieval chapter of the DSP textbook by Oppenheim and Schafer | not: phase vocoder (phase manipulation for time stretch, not magnitude-constrained inversion); inverse STFT with known phase (direct reconstruction, not iterative) [formal: iteratio Griffin-Lim | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.scope: An iterative algorithmic construct made so numerical linear algebra can solve large eigenvalue and linear-system problems without forming the full matrix.

definition.body: A Krylov subspace is a nested sequence of vector subspaces constructed from a square matrix A and a starting vector v by successive powers of A applied to v. The k-th subspace is K_k(A,v) = span{v, Av, ..., A^{k-1}v}. Parameters: (1) the square matrix A; (2) the starting vector v; (3) the subspace dimension k. Persistence mechanism: algorithmic core of iterative eigensolvers (Arnoldi, Lanczos) and linear solvers (GMRES, CG); encoded in numerical libraries (MATLAB eigs/gmres, ARPACK, SLEPc); taught in numerical linear algebra (Saad, Trefethen & Bau). e.g.: Arnoldi iteration in SciPy.sparse.linalg.eigs to compute eigenvalues of a 1000x1000 sparse matrix; GMRES in MATLAB solving a 10000x10000 system from a CFD finite-volume discretization; Lanczos tridiagonalization in SLEPc for a 500x500 symmetric Hessian in optimization | not: the full eigenspace of A (all eigenvectors, not from one starting vector); the range of A^k (column space, not generated by Krylov iteration) [formal: spatium Krylov | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

payload.name: arnoldi-algorithm
payload.scope: An iterative procedure made to build an orthonormal basis for a Krylov subspace, enabling projection methods for large sparse eigenvalue problems.

definition.body: The Arnoldi algorithm constructs an orthonormal basis Q_m for the Krylov subspace K_m(A,v) of an n×n matrix A and starting vector v. At each step k, it computes w = Av, then orthogonalizes w against all previous basis vectors q_1,...,q_{k-1} using modified Gram-Schmidt, normalizes the residual, and stores the orthogonalization coefficients as Hessenberg matrix entries H_{ij}. Parameters: (1) the square matrix A; (2) the starting vector v; (3) the subspace dimension m. Persistence mechanism: core of sparse eigensolvers (MATLAB eigs, ARPACK eigs), encoded in numerical libraries (SciPy.sparse.linalg.svds, SLEPc); taught in numerical linear algebra (Trefethen & Bau Lecture 23, Saad's Iterative Methods). e.g.: MATLAB eigss calling Arnoldi to compute 6 eigenvalues of a 5000x5000 sparse graph Laplacian; ARPACK dsaupd running Arnoldi on a 20000x20000 CFD discretization matrix to find eigenvalues nearest to a target; SciPy sparse.linalg.svds using Arnoldi bidiagonalization for 10000x10000 recommendation-system matrix factorization | not: the Lanczos algorithm (specialized for symmetric A, avoiding full reorthogonalization); the QR algorithm (iterates full-matrix QR factorizations, not Krylov projection) [formal: algorithmum Arnoldi | substrate: behavior | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]

definition.body: The Hessenberg form of a square matrix A is a matrix H = Q^T A Q that is upper Hessenberg: h_{ij} = 0 for i > j+1, so only the main diagonal, first superdiagonal, and above are nonzero.
